name: Motion

hero.title: A presence animation is one line. The compositor runs it.
hero.lede: `kinetic('div').preset(fadeUp)` gives you a component that animates in and out: fades, slides, height collapses, and staggered lists that arrive in order. It runs on CSS transitions with no JavaScript animation loop, and handles reduced motion and server rendering for you.

why.title: Motion that is cheap to run and easy to write.

items.title: One factory, immutable chains
items.text: `kinetic('div').preset(fadeUp)` is a component and a builder in one value. Every chain call returns a new component, so you define `FadeUp` once at module scope and fork variants from it.

items.title: The browser does the animating
items.text: Kinetic applies the start and end styles (or classes) across a double `requestAnimationFrame` and waits for `transitionend`. Animate `transform`, `opacity` and `filter` and the work stays on the compositor thread.

items.title: Lists that arrive in order
items.text: `.stagger({ interval: 75 })` sequences children, sets `--stagger-index` on each and can leave last-in, first-out with `reverseLeave`.

items.title: Safe for every user and every crawler
items.text: On the server, initially hidden content is emitted with its hidden style inlined, so scroll-reveal sections are in the HTML. For readers who ask for less motion, render the plain element instead of the reveal, as the recipe below does.

difference.title: The same panel, with less ceremony.

before.label: React + Motion
before.caption: A presence boundary, a conditional, a key and four animation props for one panel.

after.label: Pyreon + kinetic
after.caption: Define the animated box once. `show` takes the signal read; leave runs before it hides.

items.name: Four modes:
items.text: transition, collapse (height 0 ↔ auto), stagger and group

items.name: Style or class config:
items.text: `.enter()` / `.enterTo()` objects, or `.enterClass({ active, from, to })` for Tailwind

items.name: Lifecycle callbacks:
items.text: onEnter, onAfterEnter, onLeave and onAfterLeave, as props or through `.on()`

items.name: 122 presets:
items.text: fades, slides, zooms, flips, blur, clip-path reveals, perspective, swing and more

items.name: 5 factories:
items.text: createFade, createSlide, createScale, createRotate and createBlur with direction, distance, duration and easing

items.name: 5 utilities:
items.text: compose, withDuration, withEasing, withDelay and reverse, so you tune a preset without forking it

items.name: Stagger custom properties:
items.text: `--stagger-index` and `--stagger-interval` on every child for your own CSS timing

items.name: SSR-safe:
items.text: initially hidden content is rendered with its hidden state, not dropped

items.name: Native:
items.text: a kinetic box with a fade, scale or slide preset compiles to the primitives' Transition on iOS and Android; other presets warn by name

limits.title: Presence, not physics
limits.text: Kinetic animates elements entering and leaving. For drag-driven springs or scroll-linked timelines, pair it with a physics library; the bouncy presets use cubic-bezier curves.

limits.title: Animate transform, opacity and filter
limits.text: Width, height, top and left run on the main thread. For height, use collapse mode.

limits.title: Import presets by name
limits.text: Named imports tree-shake to what you use. The `presets` map pins all 122 (about 2.2 KB gzip, author-measured), and a misspelled `presets[name]` animates nothing without an error.

limits.title: Stagger is for lists that stay
limits.text: Stagger reads its children once at render. Group mode, for lists that change at runtime, does not yet animate removals (#4359); until it does, animate the list container rather than its rows.

limits.title: Reduced motion and reveals
limits.text: An initially hidden box that later shows stays hidden under reduced motion (#4336). Until the fix lands, gate reveals on `useReducedMotion()` and render the plain element for those readers.

comingFrom.title: Animated add and remove for a keyed list.
comingFrom.note: Group mode diffs children by `key`. Pass an accessor (`{() => …}`) so the list re-evaluates when the data changes; a plain snapshot would never animate a later addition.

recipes.title: An FAQ accordion
recipes.text: Collapse mode animates height between 0 and the measured content height, which a plain CSS transition to `auto` still cannot do in every browser.

recipes.title: A checklist that arrives in order
recipes.text: Stagger mode with `fadeUp`: each step starts 80 ms after the one before, and on hide the steps leave last-in, first-out. Readers who ask for less motion get the plain list.

recipes.title: A scroll reveal that search engines still read
recipes.text: An IntersectionObserver flips one signal. On the server the section renders with its hidden style inlined, so the heading is in the HTML. Readers who ask for less motion get the plain section.

faq.q: Why CSS transitions instead of a JavaScript animation engine?
faq.a: Because the browser already interpolates `transform`, `opacity` and `filter` off the main thread. Kinetic only decides when each phase starts and ends, so a busy main thread does not stutter the animation.
Yes. `.enterClass({ active, from, to })` and `.leaveClass()` take utility classes, and a preset can carry class fields instead of style objects.
Visuals are skipped and the element goes straight to its end state. `onEnter` → `onAfterEnter` and `onLeave` → `onAfterLeave` still fire, so logic that waits for an animation keeps working.

faq.q: Does it run on iOS and Android?
faq.a: Partly, and experimentally. A kinetic box with a fade, scale or slide preset compiles to the same native transition as `<Transition>` from `@pyreon/primitives`; presets with no native analogue warn by name. `<Transition>` is the portable spelling.

We ran kinetic against Motion and do not publish the result yet: in that run kinetic measured faster than our own hand-written CSS baseline, which the same work cannot do. Until the harness explains that, there is no claim. Don't trust us; that is the point.
